name: Visual Hierarchy
description: Governs all visual hierarchy decisions in UI — size, weight, colour contrast, emphasis, scan paths (F-pattern/Z-pattern), proximity, and grouping. Use this skill whenever the user asks about visual weight, hierarchy, emphasizing elements, de-emphasizing text, whitespace, Gestalt principles like figure/ground, or arranging elements by importance. Also trigger for any UI review task — evaluating what draws the eye is mandatory.
sourceBooks: Visual Design of the User Interface

rules.rule: Combine font weight and color contrast alongside size to establish hierarchy.
rules.why: Relying purely on size requires massive scale jumps to show distinction, which wastes space and creates clumsy proportions.
rules.check: Is the primary element distinct from the secondary element even if they were the same size?
rules.bad: A page title is 48px, a section title is 36px, and body text is 24px, all using the same regular font weight and black c
rules.good: A page title is 32px (bold, black), section title is 20px (semibold, dark gray), and body text is 16px (regular, medium

rules.rule: Soften secondary information by reducing its contrast or weight instead of making the primary information larger or bolder.
rules.why: When everything shouts, nothing is heard. Lowering the volume on less important elements makes the important ones stand out naturally.
rules.check: Did you try making the supporting text lighter before you tried making the main text bolder?
rules.bad: Making a heading bold and uppercase just because the body text below it feels too prominent.
rules.good: Changing the color of a timestamp to a lighter gray so the primary comment text stands out more.

rules.rule: Apply heavier font weights (600, 700) to data or labels you want the user to process first.
rules.why: Bold text has more visual weight and creates stronger contrast against the background, drawing the eye immediately.
rules.check: Does the most critical piece of text in this component have the heaviest font weight?
rules.bad: A dashboard stat card where the label "Total Revenue" and the number "$10,000" both use regular font weight.
rules.good: A dashboard stat card where the number "$10,000" is bold and the label "Total Revenue" is regular and gray.

rules.rule: Apply lighter colors (e.g., grays on a light background) to reduce the visual weight of tertiary information.
rules.why: Lower contrast reduces the element's "pull" on the user's attention, pushing it back in the visual hierarchy.
rules.check: Are less critical elements (like timestamps or footnotes) lower in contrast than the main content?
rules.bad: Body text and less important metadata are both rendered in `#111111` black.
rules.good: Body text is `#111111`, while the author name and date are `#666666`.

rules.rule: Style text based on its visual importance in the UI, not its semantic HTML tag (h1, h2, h3).
rules.why: A secondary label might semantically be an `h2`, but visually it might need to look smaller than body text to avoid overwhelming the layout.
rules.check: Are you styling this element based on how important it looks rather than its underlying HTML tag?
rules.bad: Forcing an `h3` category label to be 24px bold because "headings should be big", making it overpower the 18px article ti
rules.good: Styling the `h3` category label as 12px uppercase and gray, allowing the article title to dominate.

rules.rule: Place related elements closer together than unrelated elements.
rules.why: Proximity is the strongest visual cue for relationship; the brain assumes things that are close together belong together.
rules.check: Is the space between related items demonstrably smaller than the space between unrelated groups?
rules.bad: A form label is equidistant from the input field it belongs to and the input field above it.
rules.good: A form label is 4px above its input field, and there is 24px of space before the next label.

rules.rule: Surround high-priority elements with generous whitespace to increase their perceived importance.
rules.why: Empty space removes visual competition, allowing the isolated element to become the focal point.
rules.check: Does the primary action or message have the most "breathing room" in the layout?
rules.bad: A primary "Buy Now" button is crammed immediately next to a dense paragraph of terms and conditions.
rules.good: A pricing tier has ample padding around its price and a distinct "Sign Up" button separated by generous whitespace.

rules.rule: Place critical information along the top and left edges for text-heavy interfaces.
rules.why: Users from left-to-right reading cultures naturally scan across the top, then down the left side, looking for keywords.
rules.check: Are the most important headers and keywords anchored to the left edge of the content area?
rules.bad: Important status indicators are buried in the middle of a dense paragraph on a dashboard.
rules.good: A list of articles aligns titles to the left edge, with the most important metadata at the start of the line.

rules.rule: Place the primary call-to-action at the bottom right of a low-density, image-heavy layout.
rules.why: The eye sweeps horizontally across the top, diagonally down to the bottom left, and horizontally across the bottom right.
rules.check: Does the scan path terminate at the primary action button?
rules.bad: A hero section places the primary call-to-action button in the bottom left, contrary to the natural exit point.
rules.good: A landing page hero has the logo top-left, navigation top-right, headline center, and "Get Started" button bottom-right.

rules.rule: Ensure the primary element (figure) is clearly differentiated from its background (ground).
rules.why: Ambiguous figure-ground relationships cause perceptual confusion and slow down cognitive processing.
rules.check: Can you instantly tell what is the foreground object and what is the background?
rules.bad: Placing white text over a complex, light-colored photograph without an overlay.
rules.good: Using a semi-transparent dark gradient overlay on an image to ensure white text remains readable and distinct.

rules.rule: Provide just enough visual information for the user to perceive a complete pattern, reducing visual clutter.
rules.why: The human brain prefers to perceive complete shapes; leveraging this allows you to remove unnecessary borders or lines.
rules.check: Could you remove a border or line and still have the user understand the grouping?
rules.bad: Drawing a heavy box around every single item in a list to separate them.
rules.good: Using only whitespace and alignment to separate list items, relying on the user's mind to close the implicit rows.

rules.rule: Apply consistent visual treatments (color, shape, size) to elements that share the same function or category.
rules.why: Elements that look similar are perceived to be part of the same group or have the same behavior.
rules.check: Do all elements that perform the same type of action look visually identical?
rules.bad: Primary action buttons on different pages have different colors and border radii.
rules.good: All destructive actions (Delete, Remove) across the app use the same red text style.

rules.rule: Align elements linearly to lead the eye smoothly from one point of interest to another.
rules.why: Elements arranged in a line or curve are perceived as more related than elements not on the line or curve.
rules.check: Do the elements form a continuous visual path that guides the user to the next logical step?
rules.bad: A multi-step form where the "Next" button jumps between the left and right sides of the screen depending on the step.
rules.good: A timeline UI where a continuous vertical line connects chronological events, guiding the eye downward.

rules.rule: In key-value pairs, emphasize the data and de-emphasize the label.
rules.why: Users usually know what the data represents from context; the data itself is the unique, useful information.
rules.check: Does the data stand out more than the label describing it?
rules.bad: A profile card where "Email Address:" is bold and black, and `user@example.com` is regular and gray.
rules.good: A profile card where `user@example.com` is dark and regular, and "Email Address" is small, uppercase, and light gray.

rules.rule: Emphasize labels instead of data only when the user is scanning a list of items looking for a specific data point.
rules.why: When comparing items (like specs on a pricing page), the user scans for the category first, then reads the data.
rules.check: Is the user looking for a specific field across multiple items, rather than reading a single item?
rules.bad: On a tech specs comparison table, the feature name (label) is tiny and gray, while the checkmark (data) is huge and bold
rules.good: On a tech specs table, the feature name is prominent and dark, helping the user scan down the list to find "Battery Life

rules.rule: When you increase the weight or size of an element (like an icon), reduce its color contrast to maintain balance.
rules.why: An element that is both large/heavy AND high-contrast will overpower the layout.
rules.check: If an icon is placed next to text, does it steal all the attention from the text?
rules.bad: A large, solid-fill icon placed next to a small paragraph, both using full black.
rules.good: A large, solid-fill icon in a light, muted blue placed next to a dark gray paragraph, balancing the visual weight.

rules.rule: Use higher contrast colors for thin elements (borders, thin icons) to ensure they remain visible.
rules.why: Thin elements have less surface area, so they inherently carry less visual weight.
rules.check: Can you easily see the border or icon at a glance without squinting?
rules.bad: A 1px border using a very light `#f3f4f6` gray that washes out on a white background.
rules.good: A 1px border using a slightly darker `#e5e7eb` gray, or increasing the border to 2px if it must remain light.

rules.rule: Ensure every screen has one unambiguous primary element or action that holds the highest visual weight.
rules.why: Without a clear focal point, the user must expend cognitive effort figuring out what they are supposed to do or read first.
rules.check: If you blur your eyes, is there a single element that stands out above all others?
rules.bad: A landing page where the headline, the hero image, and the primary button all share equal visual prominence.
rules.good: A landing page where the "Start Free Trial" button uses a vibrant, saturated brand color while everything else is neutra
